**Plain-language definition.** Sāṃkhya begins from a practical complaint, not from curiosity: living beings are struck by suffering from three directions, ordinary remedies only postpone it, and the system claims that one particular kind of knowledge ends it permanently.

**Technical definition.** The threefold suffering (**duḥkha-traya**) is the classification of affliction into the internal or psychophysical (**ādhyātmika**), the affliction caused by other beings and the external natural order (**ādhibhautika**), and the affliction attributed to cosmic, elemental or unseen agencies (**ādhidaivika**). Sāṃkhya holds that visible and ritual means give incomplete or temporary relief, and that discriminative knowledge alone yields final, non-returning cessation.

Think of a person with a recurring illness. Painkillers work, but only for a while. A ritual cure may comfort, but the disease returns. Sāṃkhya says the same thing about existence: every remedy that operates *inside* the field of nature is itself made of nature, so it can only rearrange suffering, never abolish it. To end suffering you must step outside the field — and that step is a piece of knowledge, not an action.
Sāṃkhya holds that conscious witnesses (**puruṣa**) are many, and that their plurality is numerical rather than qualitative: each is equally pure, inactive, changeless consciousness.

Three arguments map directly onto *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 18. First, the fixed distribution of birth, death and sense-faculties: were there one witness, one birth would be every birth and all would be blind when one is blind. Second, the non-simultaneity of activity: beings act at different times and in different ways, whereas a single self would make all embodied streams act together. Third, differential constitution by the three qualities, since beings differ as luminous, active or inert in temperament. A fourth consideration — that some are released while others remain bound — is a standard supplementary inference rather than a phrase of that verse.

Śaṃkara objects that every difference cited belongs to limiting adjuncts (**upādhi**), so at most many mental streams are proved. Sāṃkhya replies that bondage and release are non-transferable, and that reflection requires distinct loci in distinct intellects.

**In simple words:** Samkhya says everything objectifiable—including mind and intellect—belongs to Prakriti. Consciousness itself is Purusa. Because neither root Prakriti nor Purusa is ordinarily perceived, the system must infer them.
> **Memory line:** three means of knowledge support two ultimate realities.

**In simple words:** Prakriti is not merely physical matter. It is the common source of body, senses, mind, ego and intellect. Its three inseparable tendencies explain clarity, motion and resistance across both psychology and cosmology.

**(1) Because what does not exist cannot be brought into being — asadakaraṇāt.** A sheer non-entity cannot be produced. No amount of causal operation can produce a hare's horn or oil from sand; production presupposes something determinate to be produced. A potter's effort can manifest a pot from clay, but it cannot manifest a square circle from nothing. *Nyāya objection:* Sāṃkhya equivocates between the absolutely non-existent and the merely not-yet-existent; Nyāya denies only that the pot exists *as a pot* before production. *Reply:* the not-yet-existent effect must still be something in the material cause, otherwise the operation would have no determinate terminus.

Sāṃkhya defends itself equally on three fronts. First, the selectivity of production is real: curd comes from milk and not from water, and only a real material continuity explains that restriction, whereas an appearance-theory leaves selectivity unexplained. Second, mutability does not disqualify nature from being ultimate, because nature is by definition the principle whose being is modification; the objection would tell only against a changeless ultimate. Sāṃkhya offers five inferences for primordial material nature. From the finitude and determinateness of things (**bhedānāṃ parimāṇāt**) it argues that the limited presupposes a subtler ground. From the uniformity running through effects (**samanvayāt**) it argues from coordinated diversity to a common material basis. From operation due to causal power (**śaktitaḥ pravṛtteś ca**, the standard reading of *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 15) it argues that determinate production requires a potent source. From the distinction between cause and effect (**kāraṇa-kārya-vibhāgāt**) it argues that manifest effects imply a subtler unmanifest cause.

**How the Advaitins react to Sāṃkhya's real transformation of nature, and how Sāṃkhya defends itself.** The Advaita reaction has three parts: an unconscious first principle cannot be the scripturally described conscious cause; a real transformation of the ultimate would make the ultimate mutable and hence dependent; and the world's dependence is better explained by superimposition than by evolution. Sāṃkhya's defence also has three parts: the continuity we observe between determinate causes and determinate effects is real and requires a real material continuity; treating the world as appearance leaves the *selectivity* of production unexplained, since appearances too would then be arbitrary; and Sāṃkhya's ultimate is not made mutable by evolution, because nature is *by definition* the principle whose being is modification, unlike a changeless Brahman.

The rivals must now be rejected. Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika holds that the effect is absent beforehand as prior non-existence (**prāgabhāva**) and that production is a new beginning; it objects that Sāṃkhya equivocates between the absolutely non-existent and the merely not-yet-existent, and that the whole (**avayavin**) is a new substance with new properties. Sāṃkhya replies that a not-yet-existent effect must still be something determinate in the cause, else the operation has no terminus, and that new properties are new arrangements (**saṃsthāna**), not new substances from non-being. Advaita agrees that being does not arise from non-being but makes the transformation apparent (**vivartavāda**); Sāṃkhya replies that an appearance-theory cannot explain why production is selective. Buddhism explains becoming by dependent origination without an enduring material root; Sāṃkhya replies that momentary series cannot ground the observed material continuity of seed and tree.

decisions.heading: SESSION 1 — WHY SĀṂKHYA EXISTS: THREEFOLD SUFFERING AND THE DEMAND FOR FINAL CESSATION

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 1 — WHY SĀṂKHYA EXISTS: THREEFOLD SUFFERING AND THE DEMAND FOR FINAL CESSATION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Sāṃkhya begins from a practical complaint, not from curiosity: living beings are struck by suffering from three directions, ordinary remedies only postpone it, and the system claims that one particular kind of knowledge ends it permanently.

**Technical definition.** The threefold suffering (**duḥkha-traya**) is the classification of affliction into the internal or psychophysical (**ādhyātmika**), the affliction caused by other beings and the external natural order (**ādhibhautika**), and the affliction attributed to cosmic, elemental or unseen agencies (**ādhidaivika**). Sāṃkhya holds that visible and ritual means give incomplete or temporary relief, and that discriminative knowledge alone yields final, non-returning cessation.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### DEFINITION / WHAT THIS IS CALLED

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: Think of a person with a recurring illness. Painkillers work, but only for a while. A ritual cure may comfort, but the disease returns. Sāṃkhya says the same thing about existence: every remedy that operates *inside* the field of nature is itself made of nature, so it can only rearrange suffering, never abolish it. To end suffering you must step outside the field — and that step is a piece of knowledge, not an action.

That single move explains the whole architecture. If liberation is by knowledge, the system must say exactly *what* is to be known. It answers: know that you are the witness and not the field. Everything else in Sāṃkhya — the two ultimates, the qualities, the twenty-five principles, the theory of causation — exists to make that one discriminative statement true and intelligible.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **Suffering is universal and threefold.** The classification is not decorative. It is designed

to be exhaustive: whatever afflicts you comes from your own psychophysical constitution, from other beings and the surrounding material order, or from agencies you cannot control or observe. If the list is exhaustive, no remedy that addresses only one arrow can be complete.

2. **Visible remedies are structurally partial.** Medicine, protection and prosperity operate within the field of nature. They redistribute conditions; they do not remove the possibility of affliction.
3. **Ritual remedies are structurally impermanent.** Anything *produced* is liable to destruction.

A result won by a sacrificial act is a produced result, so it is exhaustible and must be won again. Sāṃkhya therefore treats scripturally promised results as belonging to the same category as visible ones: better, but not final.
4. **Therefore the required remedy must be non-productive.** It cannot manufacture a new state; it
must correct a mistake. A mistake is corrected by knowledge.
5. **Hence the whole system is enumerative.** "Sāṃkhya" is traditionally connected both with

discriminative or right knowledge and with enumeration — fitting a system that promises liberation through the knowledge of twenty-five principles. The list of principles is the content of the liberating knowledge.

> **Qualification to keep.** The threefold diagnosis is a doctrinal framing rather than a separately > printed syllabus noun. It earns its place because it explains why liberation, not cosmology, is > the organising end of the entire system — and because it is what makes the enumeration of > principles a soteriological exercise rather than a taxonomy.

decisions.heading: HOW TO WRITE THE PARAGRAPH — CLAIM -> NAMED EVIDENCE -> ANALYSIS -> QUALIFICATION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Claim.** Sāṃkhya's metaphysical apparatus is generated by a therapeutic demand, not by speculative interest.

**Named evidence.** The system opens from the impact of threefold suffering — internal (**ādhyātmika**), from other beings and the material environment (**ādhibhautika**), and from cosmic or unseen agencies (**ādhidaivika**) — and rejects both visible remedies and ritual means as partial or exhaustible.

**Analysis.** Because a produced result is by definition perishable, no *action* can supply a final cure; only a correction of misidentification can, and a correction of misidentification is knowledge. This is precisely why the school must enumerate principles: the discriminative knowledge that liberates is knowledge that the witness is not any of the twenty-four evolutes.

**Qualification.** The point is not that Sāṃkhya despises ordinary or ritual remedies; it grades them. They are effective within nature and ineffective against the structural condition that makes affliction recur, which is why the school treats them as preliminary rather than false.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **Traditional lineage, honest limits.** Tradition associates the school with Kapila, followed by
Āsuri and Pañcaśikha. Their foundational works are not extant in securely recoverable form, so they are names in a lineage rather than quotable authorities.
2. **The classical baseline.** The earliest extant systematic classical text is Īśvarakṛṣṇa's
*Sāṃkhyakārikā*, with major explanatory traditions including Gauḍapāda's commentary and Vācaspati Miśra's *Tattvakaumudī*.
3. **The later phase must be labelled.** The *Sāṃkhyapravacana-sūtra* and Vijñānabhikṣu's
commentary represent a later textual and often more theistic phase. They must not be projected uncritically back into every claim of the classical Kārikā system.
4. **What the name signals.** "Sāṃkhya" is traditionally connected both with discriminative or
right knowledge and with enumeration. Both senses fit a system that seeks liberation through knowledge of twenty-five principles.
5. **Non-theism, stated precisely.** In the classical system no God is required for either bondage

or liberation. The safest formulation is that the position is *non-theistic* or *God-unproved* rather than a demonstration that no divine being could exist: primordial material nature and conscious witnesses are held sufficient for the explanatory work.
6. **The boundary with Yoga.** Sāṃkhya supplies the dualist metaphysics of primordial nature and

many witnesses that classical Yoga substantially shares. Yoga then develops a distinct practical psychology — mind-field, afflictions, meditative absorption, the eight-limbed discipline, and a special conscious witness identified as God. Therefore Yoga is a *bounded comparison* in a Sāṃkhya answer, never a source of Sāṃkhya doctrine.

**Named evidence.** Classical Sāṃkhya is fixed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa's *Sāṃkhyakārikā* and its commentarial tradition, including Vācaspati Miśra's *Tattvakaumudī*, while the *Sāṃkhyapravacana-sūtra* and Vijñānabhikṣu represent a later and often more theistic phase.

**Analysis.** The difference is doctrinally decisive: the classical system argues that primordial nature and plural witnesses are jointly sufficient to explain world, bondage and release, so importing a later God-affirming reading does not merely add a thesis — it removes the explanatory economy that the classical arguments were built to establish.

**Qualification.** The later phase is not thereby worthless; it is a legitimate development that shows the pressure Vedāntic theism exerted on the school. It simply cannot be used as evidence about what Īśvarakṛṣṇa's system held.

decisions.heading: SESSION 3 — THREE MEANS OF VALID KNOWLEDGE AND THE INFERENTIAL BURDEN

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 3 — THREE MEANS OF VALID KNOWLEDGE AND THE INFERENTIAL BURDEN

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Sāṃkhya allows only three ways of knowing anything. That decision creates a problem it must then solve, because the two things the system most needs — primordial nature and the witness — cannot be seen.

**Technical definition.** Sāṃkhya admits exactly three means of valid knowledge (**pramāṇa**): perception (**dṛṣṭa / pratyakṣa**), inference (**anumāna**) and reliable verbal testimony (**āptavacana / śabda**). Other candidates — comparison (**upamāna**), postulation (**arthāpatti**), non-apprehension (**anupalabdhi**), inclusion or probability (**sambhava**) and traditional report (**aitihya**) — are not dismissed as useless but reduced to, or included within, these three.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### DEFINITION / WHAT THIS IS CALLED

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: Imagine a court that accepts only three kinds of evidence: what the witness saw, what can be validly inferred, and the testimony of a reliable authority. Now the court must decide a case about something nobody can ever see. It cannot invent a fourth kind of evidence without abandoning its own rule. So it must show that inference alone — of a particular, carefully specified kind — is strong enough to reach the invisible defendant.

That is exactly Sāṃkhya's situation, and it is why the proofs of primordial nature and of the witness are not rhetorical flourishes. They are the discharge of a debt the school incurred when it restricted the instruments of knowledge to three.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **The three definitions, precisely.**
- **Perception** is the ascertainment with respect to a presented object (**prativiṣayādhyavasāya**)
of objects through the sense-capacities in contact with them.
- **Inference** is threefold, as tabulated above.
- **Reliable testimony** is the word of a trustworthy source, pre-eminently Veda or **śruti**, where
the speaker or text is not defective and the object is not otherwise easily known.
**Why the reductions matter.** Sāṃkhya is not being economical for its own sake. Each reduction is an argued claim:
comparison (**upamāna**) | inference / testimony | Similarity works because a prior verbal report is applied inferentially to a present case.
postulation (**arthāpatti**) | inference | Postulation is inference to the best explanatory condition; no separate instrument is needed.
non-apprehension (**anupalabdhi**) | perception's failure-conditions | Non-perception means the conditions for perceiving are absent or the object is unavailable.
inclusion / probability (**sambhava**) | inference | Moving from a larger unit to a smaller or probable implication is inferential dependence.
traditional report (**aitihya**) | testimony when reliable | Mere tradition has force only when it becomes trustworthy verbal cognition.

**Why non-perception does not refute.** Sāṃkhya lists the standard causes of non-perception: excessive distance, excessive proximity, defect of the organ, inattention of mind, subtlety (**saukṣmya**), obstruction by an intervening object, being overpowered by something else, and admixture with like things. Root nature's imperceptibility is assigned to **subtlety**; the witness is likewise beyond the senses rather than non-existent. This is the single most important defensive move in the topic: *imperceptibility is a fact about the knower's instruments, not a proof of absence.*

**Why general-correlation inference is decisive.** Ordinary inference of the first two kinds needs the invariable relation (**vyāpti**) to be established by observing both terms together. That is impossible for a term never observed at all. General-correlation inference (**sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa**) can reach such a term because it does not require the two terms to be seen together; it works through a general correlation of *kinds*. Since perception cannot reach what is beyond the senses, and testimony alone would beg the question against non-Vedic opponents, the argumentative burden falls here.
**Objections and replies.**
- **Cārvāka objection.** The invariable relation cannot be secured for a term never perceived;

inference to root nature or the witness is therefore speculative. **Reply.** Strict perceptualism cannot explain ordinary causal reasoning either; manifest, dependent, purposive and objectifiable experience demands an unmanifest material ground and a conscious witness.
- **Nyāya objection.** General-correlation inference is legitimate, but Sāṃkhya overuses it. A

plurality of atoms plus an intelligent God explains the ordered world more economically than an unobservable material first cause. **Reply.** The continuity between cause and effect, the qualitative character of experience and the determinacy of production are better explained by a single material nature; adding God is unnecessary because it does not explain the material continuity itself.

> **Presupposition to state openly.** Sāṃkhya presupposes that inference from general correlation > can legitimately reach an entity of a kind never itself observed as a sense-object. If that > presupposition is denied, the five proofs of primordial nature become analogical guesses rather > than philosophical inferences.

decisions.heading: HOW TO WRITE THE PARAGRAPH — CLAIM -> NAMED EVIDENCE -> ANALYSIS -> QUALIFICATION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Claim.** Sāṃkhya's restriction to three instruments of knowledge is what makes its metaphysical proofs necessary rather than ornamental.

**Named evidence.** The school admits only perception, inference and reliable testimony, reducing comparison, postulation, non-apprehension, inclusion and traditional report to these three; and it classes root nature's imperceptibility under subtlety (**saukṣmya**) in the standard list of eight causes of non-perception.

**Analysis.** Because both ultimates are beyond the senses and testimony would be question-begging against a non-Vedic opponent, the entire evidential weight falls on general-correlation inference (**sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa**), which alone can reach a term whose invariable relation was never observed directly. The five proofs of nature and the five proofs of the witness are therefore the exact shape this epistemology forces.

**Qualification.** The move is powerful but not cost-free: it rests on the presupposition that a general correlation of kinds can license an inference to an entity of a kind never observed, and it is precisely this presupposition that Cārvāka denies and Nyāya accepts while accusing Sāṃkhya of over-extending it.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 4 — COGNITION: THE INNER INSTRUMENT, REFLECTION AND APPARENT AGENCY

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** In Sāṃkhya the mind is not conscious and consciousness does not think. Knowing happens when an insentient mental organ takes the shape of an object and the witness's light falls on it — so the event *looks* like a conscious mind knowing, although neither of its two components is that.

**Technical definition.** The inner instrument (**antaḥkaraṇa**) has three functions — determinative intellect (**buddhi**), the I-maker (**ahaṃkāra**) and the coordinating mind (**manas**). With the five cognitive capacities and five action capacities it forms the thirteenfold instrument (**trayodaśa-karaṇa**). Intellect alone makes the final ascertainment (**adhyavasāya**). Being predominantly luminous (**sattva**-predominant), intellect receives the reflection of the witness (**puruṣa-cchāyā-āpatti / buddhi-pratibimba**), and this reflection generates false appropriation (**abhimāna**) — "I am the doer, knower, enjoyer" — which is the psychological root of bondage.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### DEFINITION / WHAT THIS IS CALLED

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: Think of a clean mirror in a dark room and a lamp outside the doorway. The mirror cannot glow; the lamp cannot take shapes. But put them in the right relation and you get something that looks exactly like a glowing image. Sāṃkhya says empirical knowing is that: the intellect takes the shape of the object, the witness supplies the light, and the resulting cognition seems to be a conscious mind's own act.

Two mistakes then become natural. The insentient organ appears conscious, and the inactive witness appears to be an agent. Both mistakes are one mistake seen from two ends — and undoing it is what liberation means.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **Three inner functions, sharply distinguished.** Intellect determines and ascertains; the

functions as doorkeeper (**dvārin**) because it receives, coordinates and determines what enters cognition. Sense-capacities present; only intellect concludes.
3. **Only intellect ascertains.** Final ascertainment (**adhyavasāya**) belongs to intellect alone.
This matters for the exam because the 2024 question asks precisely for the difference between cosmic intellect, determinative intellect and the I-maker.
4. **Why intellect and not another organ receives the reflection.** Intellect is
**sattva**-predominant and therefore transparent. Transparency is what makes reflection possible; a **tamas**-heavy organ would obstruct rather than receive.
5. **The two-way appearance.** Through conjunction or the semblance of conjunction, the unconscious
internal instrument appears conscious, while the inactive witness appears to be an agent. Productive agency belongs to the qualities and evolutes of nature; witnessing belongs to the witness.
6. **From reflection to bondage.** The reflection generates false appropriation (**abhimāna**) — "I

am the doer/knower/enjoyer" — and that appropriation is the psychological root of bondage. Note the exact ordering: reflection is a structural fact, appropriation is the error, bondage is the consequence.

decisions.heading: SESSION 5 — PRIMORDIAL MATERIAL NATURE: WHAT IT IS AND WHY THE SYSTEM NEEDS IT

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 5 — PRIMORDIAL MATERIAL NATURE: WHAT IT IS AND WHY THE SYSTEM NEEDS IT

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Primordial material nature is the one unconscious stuff out of which everything objective evolves — not only bodies and elements, but also intellect, ego, mind and the senses. It is never created and never perceived; it is inferred as the root of everything that changes.

**Technical definition.** Primordial material nature (**prakṛti**) is the unmanifest, unconscious, primordial material principle from which the entire objective and psychophysical world evolves. It is called the chief principle (**pradhāna**) because it is the primary material basis of all empirical manifestation, and the unmanifest (**avyakta**) because in its primordial condition it is not yet differentiated into manifest principles. It is the ultimate material cause of the world within Sāṃkhya's dualist ontology.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### DEFINITION / WHAT THIS IS CALLED

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: Two words will keep you out of trouble here. First, *material* in Sāṃkhya does not mean "physical". Intellect, ego, mind and the senses are all products of nature; they are unconscious machinery, however subtle. Second, *root* does not mean "first event". Nature is not a beginning in time; it is the standing condition from which manifestation issues whenever equilibrium is disturbed.

So when you write "nature", picture a single reservoir of unconscious potency that includes the mind, not a heap of matter opposed to the mind. Getting this right prevents the commonest error in the topic: reading Sāṃkhya as a mind–body dualism instead of a consciousness–nature dualism.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Why a second principle is required at all.**
1. The world is marked by plurality, transformation, dependence, purposiveness and structured
manifestation.
2. A school that accepts real effects, real bondage and real liberation needs a real material
source from which empirical diversity emerges. Sāṃkhya is a realist; it cannot dissolve the world into appearance.
3. The witness is changeless and inactive, so it cannot itself become the world. A changeless
principle that turned into the world would not be changeless.
4. Therefore a second principle is required: active but unconscious nature.
**The three names, and what each licenses in an answer.**
**prakṛti** | the productive nature of the principle | the general term
**pradhāna** | it is the *chief* material principle | Śaṃkara's target term in **pradhāna malla**
**avyakta** | it is *unmanifest* before differentiation | contrasts with the manifest (**vyakta**) evolutes

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **(1) From the finitude and determinateness of things — bhedānāṃ parimāṇāt.** Empirical things are many, finite, delimited and measurable. What is finite and determinate points beyond itself to a more fundamental source from which such determinate forms arise; the manifold world therefore requires a common antecedent material ground. The force of the argument is not merely "every effect has a cause", but that *the limited and differentiated presuppose a subtler ground from which limitation and differentiation emerge*.

**(2) From the uniformity running through effects — samanvayāt.** Effects display an underlying order and common pattern; diverse products nevertheless reveal continuity of constitution and dependence. Such systematic coherence suggests a common material basis. This is an argument from *coordinated* diversity: if effects hang together, they are likely rooted in one underlying matrix.

**(3) From operation due to causal power — śaktitaḥ pravṛtteś ca.** Effects arise through the operation of a cause possessing the relevant power (**śakti**). Evolution is manifestation of what the potent cause can produce; an impotent or unrelated source cannot generate a determinate effect. Therefore the world-process presupposes an underlying productive power capable of the full range of manifest effects.

> **Textual control — write this if you can.** The standard reading of *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 15 is > **śaktitaḥ pravṛtteś ca**, not *kāryataḥ pravṛtteḥ*. The argument is from causal power and > operation, **not** from conscious purposive planning. Getting this right is what stops the proof > collapsing into a design argument — which would be fatal for a non-theistic system.

**(4) From the distinction between cause and effect — kāraṇa-kārya-vibhāgāt.** Cause and effect are distinguishable stages: the unmanifest source and the manifest product are not identical in appearance. If effects are manifest, multiple and differentiated, their cause must be a more basic, prior and subtler condition. The point is not total disconnection; cause and effect are distinguishable without being unrelated.

**(5) From the undivided source of the diversified universe — avibhāgāt vaiśvarūpyasya.** The world is astonishingly diverse, yet this diversity forms **one interconnected cosmos**. A diversified whole points back to an undivided source in which later differentiations are not yet separated. Therefore there must be an original unmanifest, undivided root of the whole world-process. **This is the proof that shows nature must be ONE**, and it is the strongest anti-pluralist argument at the level of material causation in the system.

**The 2019 answer, stated exactly.** The proof is **avibhāgāt vaiśvarūpyasya**. Reason: if the entire articulated universe emerges from an undivided source, that source must itself be singular, not many independent primal materials. In a ten-marker, do not merely name the proof — add the logical bridge: *plurality at the root would undermine the very inference to an undivided source of total cosmic diversity.*

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 7 — THE THREE QUALITIES, EQUILIBRIUM AND MODIFICATION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Nature is not a smooth blank; it is woven from three strands that are always present together in different proportions. Change the proportion and you change the object, the mood and the moral tone at once. Balance the three exactly and nothing manifests at all.

**Technical definition.** The three qualities (**guṇa**) are luminosity (**sattva**), activity (**rajas**) and inertia (**tamas**). They are not three separable substances but three inseparable constitutive tendencies within one nature. Their exact balance is the state of equilibrium (**sāmyāvasthā**), in which nature remains unmanifest. Transformation within each quality's own nature is homogeneous modification (**sarūpa-pariṇāma**); asymmetrical transformation producing differentiated evolutes is heterogeneous modification (**virūpa-pariṇāma**).

Sāṃkhya infers a conscious support in whose presence the unconscious system becomes an experienced order. **This is not a God-proof**; it is an inference to the witness as the presiding witness of lived order. Marking this explicitly is worth marks, because it is the point at which a careless answer accidentally imports theism into a non-theistic system.

**(4) Experience requires an enjoyer — bhoktṛ-bhāvāt.** Pleasure, pain and delusion are experienced. Since these are presented as objects or states, there must be an experiencer (**bhoktṛ**) distinct from them. Unconscious nature can *present* experience, but it cannot be the subject *for whom* experience appears.

**(5) Striving for liberation presupposes a liberable witness — kaivalyārthaṃ pravṛtteḥ.** Human striving for release from suffering is a central fact for Sāṃkhya. Such striving would be unintelligible if there were no conscious principle distinct from bondage-producing nature. The orientation toward isolation (**kaivalya**) therefore presupposes the witness.
**Evaluation — what "examine and evaluate" wants.**
- The proofs are **cumulative, not isolated**. Any one alone is answerable; together they argue that
aggregates are instrumental, qualities are objectifiable, experience requires a witness, and liberation presupposes a self.
- Their epistemic form is uniform: general-correlation inference (**sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa anumāna**), from
the general structure of objectifiable experience to a witness that is never itself an object.
- Their honest limit: they establish that experience has a *subject-pole*; they do not by themselves
establish that the subject-pole is eternal, plural or inactive. Those come from further argument (Session 9) and from the system's soteriological requirements.
**The nature of the witness, tabulated.**
Consciousness | essence, not quality
Activity | inactive, non-productive
Change | changeless, immutable
Relation to the qualities | entirely beyond them
Status | witness, seer, experiencer

Two consequences follow immediately and must be written: the witness does not become bound in its own nature — bondage belongs to misidentification; and the witness does not produce the world — all production belongs to nature.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **The ordered list.**
1 | **primordial nature (prakṛti)** | root material cause
2 | **the great one / determinative intellect (mahat / buddhi)** | first evolute
3 | **I-maker (ahaṃkāra)** | principle of individuation
4 | **coordinating mind (manas)** | internal coordinator

15–19 | **five subtle elements (tanmātra)** | subtle elements
20–24 | **five gross elements (mahābhūta)** | gross elements
25 | **conscious witness (puruṣa)** | pure consciousness, non-evolute
**The complete instrument and element taxonomy.**
Five cognitive capacities | hearing (**śrotra**), touch (**tvak**), sight (**cakṣus**), taste (**rasanā**), smell (**ghrāṇa**) | disclose sound, touch, form or colour, taste and smell
Five action capacities | speech (**vāk**), grasping (**pāṇi**), locomotion (**pāda**), excretion (**pāyu**), reproduction (**upastha**) | perform the five principal outward functions

Five subtle elements | sound-potential (**śabda**), touch-potential (**sparśa**), form-potential (**rūpa**), taste-potential (**rasa**), smell-potential (**gandha**) | arise from the inert side of the I-maker with active-quality energy
Five gross elements | ether (**ākāśa**), air (**vāyu**), fire or light (**tejas**), water (**ap**), earth (**pṛthivī**) | arise from the subtle-element series and compose the gross world

The standard correspondence runs sound → ether, touch → air, form → fire, taste → water and smell → earth. Do **not** import Advaita's later fivefold grossification (**pañcīkaraṇa**) into a basic classical Sāṃkhya evolution answer.
**The fourfold cause–effect classification — the fastest control on the whole list.**
Cause but not effect (evolvent only) | primordial nature alone | 1
Both cause and effect | intellect, I-maker and the five subtle elements | 7
Effect only | mind, five cognitive capacities, five action capacities, five gross elements | 16
Neither cause nor effect | the conscious witness | 1
This classification is the quickest way to control the full sequence and to prevent miscounting the cosmic and determinative intellect as two separate principles.
**Cosmic intellect, determinative intellect and the I-maker — the 2024 second half.**
- The great one (**mahat**) and the determinative intellect (**buddhi**) are the **same principle**.
The great one is the cosmic aspect or name; the determinative intellect is the individual or psychological aspect or name.
- The I-maker (**ahaṃkāra**) emerges **from** that principle as the principle of individuation or
I-sense.
- Therefore the sequence is nature → the great one / determinative intellect → the I-maker.
- **This is a classic trap.** Never write the great one and the determinative intellect as two
separate stages.
**What each of the three does.**
- The determinative intellect determines, judges, ascertains and discriminates; it is the locus
where reflected consciousness is most conspicuous in empirical life.
- The I-maker appropriates functions into the form "I know", "I act", "I experience"; false selfhood
crystallises here, which is why it is central to bondage.
- The mind coordinates. In one line: *mind coordinates, I-maker appropriates, intellect determines.*
**The three lines.**
- From the luminous aspect of the I-maker arise the mind, the five cognitive capacities and the five
action capacities. This line accounts for the cognitive and conative equipment of empirical life.
- From the inert aspect of the I-maker arise the five subtle elements, and from those the five gross
elements. This line accounts for subtle-to-gross material manifestation.
- The active quality supplies activity, energy and operative force to **both** lines. The
active-aspect I-maker does **not** produce a separate set of principles. Write this explicitly; it is repeatedly confused.

**Why the sequence matters philosophically.** The sequence shows that cosmology and psychology are internally linked in Sāṃkhya: the same nature that yields matter also yields the faculties through which matter is experienced. That is the philosophical point a 20-mark answer must reach after narrating the list.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Claim.** The Sāṃkhya evolutionary sequence is ordered by a single principle — subtler and more internal before grosser and more external — and that ordering is what carries its philosophical point.

**Named evidence.** Nature yields the great one or determinative intellect, which yields the I-maker, from whose luminous aspect arise the mind and the ten capacities and from whose inert aspect arise the five subtle elements and then the five gross elements, with the active quality supplying energy to both lines and producing no separate set; the fourfold classification fixes this as one evolvent, seven both, sixteen effects only, and one neither.

**Analysis.** Because determination precedes individuation and individuation precedes both the sensory apparatus and the elements, Sāṃkhya locates the "I" inside nature rather than at its origin — which is exactly what allows bondage to be described as a misplacement within the series and liberation as its correction.

**Qualification.** The order is a doctrinal derivation, not an observational chronology; the school does not claim that intellect existed before elements in datable time, but that the manifest world is intelligible only if the more determinate is derived from the less determinate.

```text

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **(1) Because what does not exist cannot be brought into being — asadakaraṇāt.** A sheer non-entity cannot be produced. No amount of causal operation can produce a hare's horn or oil from sand; production presupposes something determinate to be produced. A potter's effort can manifest a pot from clay, but it cannot manifest a square circle from nothing. *Nyāya objection:* Sāṃkhya equivocates between the absolutely non-existent and the merely not-yet-existent; Nyāya denies only that the pot exists *as a pot* before production. *Reply:* the not-yet-existent effect must still be something in the material cause, otherwise the operation would have no determinate terminus.

**(2) Because a determinate material cause is taken up — upādāna-grahaṇāt.** Specific effects require specific material causes. One who wants curd takes milk, not water; one who wants cloth takes threads, not clay. The selection of mango seed rather than sand for a mango tree shows a determinate causal base. *Objection:* the restriction may be explained by causal capacity rather than by the pre-existence of the effect. *Reply:* causal capacity in the required determinate sense just is the latent presence of that effect in that material continuum.

**(3) Because everything cannot arise from everything — sarvasambhavābhāvāt.** If effects were wholly non-existent before production, any cause could produce any effect. Non-existence as such is indistinguishable; therefore it cannot explain why curd arises from milk and not from water. Cloth comes from threads, not from milk; curd comes from milk, not from threads. *Objection:* restrictions come from the constitution of causes, not from effects already existing in causes. *Reply:* a constitution capable of producing only one effect is precisely the latent presence of that effect as a determinate effect-potential.

**(4) Because the efficient can produce only what it is capable of producing — śaktasya śakya-karaṇāt.** A cause has a determinate potency (**śakti**) directed toward a determinate effect. A potency for something is unintelligible unless that something is in some manner already there as the object of the potency. Milk has the potency for curd, not for cloth; threads have the potency for cloth, not for curd. *Nyāya objection:* potency is a relational property of the cause, not the effect in latent form. *Reply:* a merely relational potency cannot explain determinate production unless the producible form is already grounded in the material cause.

**(5) Because the effect has the nature or being of the cause — kāraṇa-bhāvāt.** The effect is non-different from the cause in substance. Cloth is nothing over and above threads in a certain arrangement; it has the same material basis, weight and quality-continuity. Ornament and gold differ in form and name, but the material substance remains gold. *Nyāya objection:* the whole (**avayavin**) is a new substance with new properties — a cloth covers, but separate threads do not. *Reply:* the new properties are new arrangements or configurations (**saṃsthāna**), not new substances created out of non-being.

> **The formulation to memorise for the mango-seed question.** Write it as *latent effect + material > continuity + real transformation*. Do **not** write it as a miniature gross mango tree hidden > inside the seed.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Claim.** Sāṃkhya's case for the pre-existent effect rests on the observed determinacy of production rather than on any claim that effects are visible inside their causes.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **What real transformation asserts.** Sāṃkhya's pre-existence doctrine is specifically the doctrine of real transformation: the effect is a real transformation of the cause. It is **not** apparent transformation, because the world is not a mere appearance superimposed on an unchanged cause; it is the real evolution of nature. The mechanism is the modification of the qualities: the three qualities transform and recombine to produce the differentiated principles. In equilibrium each quality transforms homogeneously within its own nature; when equilibrium is disturbed the qualities transform heterogeneously and generate the manifest evolutes.
**Three standing objections and their replies.**

If the effect already exists, causal effort becomes pointless. | Production is manifestation (**abhivyakti**) of what is latent; effort removes obstruction and supplies conditions — it does not create being out of non-being.
The doctrine abolishes the distinction between cause and effect. | Cause and effect differ by **state (avasthā)**: the cause is latent or unmanifest, the effect patent or manifest.
The doctrine implies the world was always exactly as it is now. | The gross effect is *not* already manifest; only the determinate capacity or effect-form exists latently in the cause.
**Contrast with apparent transformation (Advaita).**
Type of transformation | real | apparent
Technical term | **pariṇāma** | **vivarta**
Cause | primordial nature | Brahman
Status of the world | real evolute | ultimately appearance
Both may be placed under a broad pre-existence orientation, but their accounts of transformation differ radically. This is the exact point on which the 2018 fifteen-marker turns.

**How the Advaitins react to Sāṃkhya's real transformation of nature, and how Sāṃkhya defends itself.** The Advaita reaction has three parts: an unconscious first principle cannot be the scripturally described conscious cause; a real transformation of the ultimate would make the ultimate mutable and hence dependent; and the world's dependence is better explained by superimposition than by evolution. **Contrast with the non-pre-existent effect (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika).**
Effect before production | pre-existent in the cause | absent as effect — prior non-existence (**prāgabhāva**)
Production | manifestation | new beginning
Causal model | continuity through transformation | the effect as a fresh product
This contrast is directly relevant to the routed 2023 question on prior non-existence and Sāṃkhya causation, and to the routed 2021 question "Does the seed contain the tree?".

**Contrast with dependent origination (Buddhism).** Buddhism explains becoming through dependent origination rather than an enduring unmanifest material root; Sāṃkhya explains becoming through the transformation of enduring nature. A crisp contrast line is usually enough unless the question explicitly asks for a Buddhist comparison.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **1. Bondage.** Bondage is non-discrimination between the witness and nature. The intellect reflects consciousness, and this reflection creates false identification; the self then appears as agent, enjoyer, sufferer and knower in the empirical sense. Bondage is **not** a real alteration in the witness but mistaken identification through reflected consciousness.

**2. Liberation.** Liberation is discriminative knowledge — the knowledge that "I am not nature". When the distinction between witness-consciousness and quality-evolutes becomes steady, false identification ends. This state is isolation, the aloneness of the witness. Isolation is not merger; it is disentanglement.

**3. The lame-and-blind image.** The witness is like the lame man: conscious but inactive. Nature is like the blind man: active but unconscious. Together they explain empirical process. The image conveys complementarity without collapsing the two principles into one.

**4. The dancer image.** Nature is like a dancer who stops after being seen by the witness. Once discriminative knowledge arises, nature no longer continues its binding display for that witness. This is the neatest canonical image for liberation through fulfilled disclosure.

**5. Two stages of release.** Liberation while the body still continues, due to prior momentum, is **jīvanmukti**; the standard analogy is the potter's wheel that keeps turning even after the impulse ceases. Final cessation of embodiment, when the body falls and residual momentum ends, is **videhamukti**.

**6. The strict textual nuance.** This is stronger than "the witness becomes free": in strict Sāṃkhya the conscious witness is never really bound, liberated or transmigrating. These processes belong to nature and the subtle body, while discriminative knowledge ends false attribution. In Sāṃkhya this remains isolation of consciousness, not union with God.

**7. Non-theism, argued.** No God is required for either bondage or liberation in classical Sāṃkhya. Nature's purposive evolution for the witness's experience and release is treated as sufficient. The classical position is better described as non-theistic or God-unproved than as a proof that no divine being can exist: primordial nature and conscious witnesses are held sufficient for the explanatory work. The five standard supporting arguments are set out in the visual above and should be reproduced as numbered points.

**8. Two boundary cautions.** Later Sāṃkhya writers such as Vijñānabhikṣu develop more theistic interpretations; do not project them back into Īśvarakṛṣṇa's classical non-theistic system. And this is precisely why classical Sāṃkhya must be clearly separated from Yoga, which adds a special conscious witness identified as God and owns the practical discipline.

**9. Isolation is not the same as the rival goals.** Isolation is the aloneness of the witness; release in Advaita is identity with Brahman; release in Nyāya is the cessation of suffering. Three different goals with three different technical names.

**E. Why Sāṃkhya is the chief opponent.** Three reasons, all of which must be written.
1. It is the most sophisticated non-Vedāntic rival at the level of ultimate explanation, explaining
world, self, bondage, liberation and causation through a coherent metaphysical system. It is therefore not marginal but philosophically near enough to require detailed refutation.
2. Real transformation is the nearest rival to apparent transformation. Both aim to explain the world
from an ultimate principle; Sāṃkhya takes transformation as real while Advaita takes it as apparent. This causal proximity is one reason Śaṃkara treats Sāṃkhya as chief opponent.
3. Both appeal to a single ultimate explanatory ground — Sāṃkhya through one primal material
principle, Advaita through conscious Brahman. Because both are large-scale metaphysical explanations, the contest is direct.

**F. Śaṃkara's four objections.** Unconscious nature cannot be the Upaniṣadic cause, because the scriptural source is described as conscious, knowing and of the character of being-and-consciousness. The contact problem remains unresolved. Teleology cannot be explained without consciousness. And texts describing the cause as knowing exclude an insentient nature.

**G. Exam conclusion.** Śaṃkara calls Sāṃkhya his chief opponent because it is the strongest rival causal-metaphysical system; he rejects it because the ultimate cause must be conscious, teleology cannot rest on unconscious nature, and the witness–nature relation remains unstable.
**H. Inter-school placement — the debate axes.**
Self | many witnesses | Advaita | one self/Brahman versus many witnesses
Causation | pre-existent effect + real transformation | Nyāya | pre-existent effect versus prior non-existence and new beginning
World-process | rooted in nature | Buddhism | enduring material root versus dependent origination
God | non-theistic | Yoga / Nyāya / Vedānta | no God needed versus explicit God or Brahman
Liberation | isolation | Advaita / Nyāya | isolation versus identity versus cessation of suffering
In cross-school answers Sāṃkhya is often the benchmark for real causation and for strict consciousness–matter dualism.

**I. Sāṃkhya against Cārvāka.** The contrast is worth one line in any epistemology-facing answer. Cārvāka admits perception alone and therefore rejects the inference to imperceptible entities; Sāṃkhya admits three instruments and rests its two ultimates on general-correlation inference. The Sāṃkhya reply to the Cārvāka is that strict perceptualism cannot explain ordinary causal reasoning either.

**J. Sāṃkhya against Yoga, stated as a friendly amendment.** Yoga retains the broad metaphysics of nature, the qualities and many witnesses, but adds God, a stronger practical discipline, devotion to God and the yogi's perception. Hence Sāṃkhya is non-theistic and more theoretical, while Yoga is theistic and more practical.
**K. The four standing criticisms and Sāṃkhya's replies.**

Teleology without intelligence: how can unconscious nature evolve purposively? | Purposive functioning need not involve conscious planning; the quality-structure itself yields ordered manifestation in the presence of the witness. | Preserves system-internal sufficiency but remains vulnerable to Vedāntic criticism.

Relation between two absolutes: if the two are radically different, how can misidentification occur? | Through proximity, reflection and false attribution rather than real fusion. | Partly explanatory and partly analogical; critics see it as the school's weakest point.

Multiplicity of witnesses is unnecessary: could not one consciousness appear as many? | Non-simultaneous liberation, individual experience and differentiated embodiment support plurality. | Advaita's limiting-adjunct reply is not thereby answered.

The pre-existence doctrine removes novelty: if the effect exists, production is redundant. | Production is manifestation from latent to patent, not pointless repetition. | Nyāya can still press that new properties mark a genuinely new substance.
**L. The graded verdict.**

*What is strong.* Sāṃkhya is a rigorously argued non-theistic realism rather than a loose mythology of evolution. Its theory of the qualities is one of the most economical Indian accounts of qualitative variety. The pre-existence doctrine is a genuinely powerful causal thesis because it explains determinate production and material continuity. Its separation of consciousness from mental function anticipates the modern distinction between phenomenal consciousness and cognitive processing.

*What is weak.* The witness–nature relation is under-explained. Unconscious teleology remains difficult. The individuation of attributeless witnesses is the weakest point in the plurality doctrine. The beginning of bondage is obscure, because the witness is never really modified and nature is beginningless.

*What is genuinely contested.* Whether early Sāṃkhya was originally theistic or consistently non-theistic remains debated. Whether isolation is purely negative or has a positive phenomenological character is disputed. The relation between the Kārikā tradition and the later Sūtra tradition is historically and doctrinally contested.

*Ready verdicts by length.* At ten marks: Sāṃkhya is strongest as a concise dualist realism — one nature explains the world, many witnesses explain experience, discrimination explains liberation. At fifteen: its power lies in the mutual fit of instruments of knowledge, the pre-existent effect, the theory of the qualities and isolation, though the contact problem invites Vedāntic criticism. At twenty: it is a philosophically serious non-theistic system whose causal realism and psychology of reflection are impressive, but whose unconscious teleology and plurality of attributeless witnesses remain unresolved pressure points.

decisions.heading: HOW TO WRITE THE PARAGRAPH — CLAIM -> NAMED EVIDENCE -> ANALYSIS -> QUALIFICATION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Claim.** Śaṃkara's designation of Sāṃkhya as chief opponent is a judgement about systematic strength, and his refutation targets the exact point at which that strength becomes instability.

**Named evidence.** Sāṃkhya answers the relation question by mere proximity (**sānnidhya**), supported by the magnet moving iron and the crystal coloured by a nearby flower; Śaṃkara replies that a magnet exerts force and so cannot model an inactive witness, that a crystal explains appearance but not initiation, and that the scripturally described cause is conscious and knowing.

**Analysis.** The critique is well aimed because Sāṃkhya's two analogies do different jobs and neither does both: activation by presence and appearance without change are separate explananda, so the school has two partial models where it needs one complete account of how the world-process begins.

**Qualification.** Śaṃkara's own alternative is not thereby established by this argument alone; what follows is that Sāṃkhya's dualism is unstable — tending either toward monism or toward a third mediating principle — which is a demand for further explanation rather than a demonstration that the Advaita account is correct.
