excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### VERIFIED PREVIOUS-YEAR QUESTIONS — 13 COMPLETE SOLUTIONS
Ten questions are primary-owned by this syllabus item across 2018–2025; three further questions are

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: > **Printed question.** Is Puruṣa one or many? Explain the Sāṃkhya position in this regard and give > arguments in support of your answer.

**Demand decoded.** "Is … one or many" requires a verdict in the first line. "Explain … and give arguments in support" requires the canonical arguments with their source status, plus a defence against the obvious rival.
**Model answer (183 words).**
Sāṃkhya holds that conscious witnesses (**puruṣa**) are many, and that their plurality is numerical rather than qualitative: each is equally pure, inactive, changeless consciousness.

Three arguments map directly onto *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 18. First, the fixed distribution of birth, death and sense-faculties: were there one witness, one birth would be every birth and all would be blind when one is blind. Second, the non-simultaneity of activity: beings act at different times and in different ways, whereas a single self would make all embodied streams act together. Third, differential constitution by the three qualities, since beings differ as luminous, active or inert in temperament. A fourth consideration — that some are released while others remain bound — is a standard supplementary inference rather than a phrase of that verse.

Śaṃkara objects that every difference cited belongs to limiting adjuncts (**upādhi**), so at most many mental streams are proved. Sāṃkhya replies that bondage and release are non-transferable, and that reflection requires distinct loci in distinct intellects.
The argument is therefore strong morally and weak metaphysically: Sāṃkhya establishes that experience is non-transferable, but cannot state what individuates attributeless witnesses.
> **Printed question.** How do the Advaita Vedāntins react to the Prakṛtipariṇāmavāda of the > Sāṃkhya philosophy? How do the Sāṃkhyas defend their own position in this regard? Discuss.
**Demand decoded.** Two directed halves — the Advaita reaction, then the Sāṃkhya defence — held together by "Discuss", which asks for ordered exposition ending in a judgement.
**Model answer (281 words).**

Sāṃkhya's doctrine of the real transformation of primordial nature holds that the effect pre-exists in its material cause and is genuinely manifested through the modification of the three qualities: in equilibrium each quality transforms homogeneously, and on disturbance the qualities transform heterogeneously to yield the manifest principles.

Advaita reacts on three fronts. First, an unconscious first principle cannot be the cause described in the Upaniṣads, where the source is spoken of as conscious and knowing. Second, an ultimate that really transforms becomes mutable, and a mutable principle is dependent rather than ultimate; the world's dependence is therefore better explained by superimposition. Third, Advaita substitutes apparent transformation (**vivarta**) for real transformation, so that Brahman is the cause without undergoing change, as a rope is the "cause" of the snake seen in it.

Sāṃkhya defends itself equally on three fronts. First, the selectivity of production is real: curd comes from milk and not from water, and only a real material continuity explains that restriction, whereas an appearance-theory leaves selectivity unexplained. Second, mutability does not disqualify nature from being ultimate, because nature is by definition the principle whose being is modification; the objection would tell only against a changeless ultimate. Third, treating the world as appearance purchases the immutability of the cause at the cost of the reality of bondage and release, which Sāṃkhya's realism refuses to surrender.
Both schools deny production from sheer non-being, so the dispute is not about the pre-existent effect but about the reality of the transformation.

The exchange therefore terminates in a clash of first principles: Sāṃkhya preserves the reality of the world and pays with a mutable ultimate, while Advaita preserves an immutable ultimate and pays with the ultimate unreality of the world.
> **Printed question.** Critically discuss the metaphysical status of a Jīva and a Puruṣa according > to Sāṃkhya philosophy.
**Demand decoded.** "Critically discuss" requires the distinction, its mechanism, and a stated difficulty — not two definitions placed side by side.
**Model answer (186 words).**

For Sāṃkhya the conscious witness (**puruṣa**) is the metaphysical reality: pure, self-luminous, inactive and changeless consciousness, wholly beyond the three qualities. The empirical self (**jīva**) is **not a further principle** in the enumeration of twenty-five; it is the witness as empirically conditioned through identification with intellect, I-maker, mind, body and the karmic stream.

The mechanism is reflection. The determinative intellect, being predominantly luminous and therefore transparent, receives the reflection of the witness; the resulting cognition generates false appropriation (**abhimāna**) — "I am the doer, knower, enjoyer". The insentient organ thus appears conscious while the inactive witness appears to be an agent. The empirical self is precisely that two-way appearance stabilised into an apparent person.
Two consequences follow. Bondage is misidentification rather than a real modification of the witness, and liberation is the correction of attribution rather than the destruction of an entity.

Critically, the account is elegant but exposed: if the witness is never really conditioned, it becomes unclear in what sense there was ever a problem for it, and Sāṃkhya's reply — that the problem was always one of attribution — clarifies the question rather than demonstrating an answer.
> **Printed question.** Which Sāṃkhya proof for the existence of Prakṛti actually shows that there > can be only one Prakṛti? Justify your answer.
**Demand decoded.** A single named proof, then a justification. Marks are lost by listing all five without discriminating, and by naming the proof without the bridging argument.
**Model answer (272 words).**
The proof is **avibhāgāt vaiśvarūpyasya** — the argument from the undivided source of the diversified universe.

Sāṃkhya offers five inferences for primordial material nature. From the finitude and determinateness of things (**bhedānāṃ parimāṇāt**) it argues that the limited presupposes a subtler ground. From the uniformity running through effects (**samanvayāt**) it argues from coordinated diversity to a common material basis. From operation due to causal power (**śaktitaḥ pravṛtteś ca**, the standard reading of *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 15) it argues that determinate production requires a potent source. From the distinction between cause and effect (**kāraṇa-kārya-vibhāgāt**) it argues that manifest effects imply a subtler unmanifest cause.

Each of these four is compatible with a plurality of material roots. Several reservoirs could each be subtler than their products, each display internal pattern, each possess productive power, and each differ in stage from its effects. None of the four takes unity as its premise, so none can deliver unity as its conclusion.

The fifth argument alone does. It begins from the observation that cosmic diversity is not a heap but one interconnected whole, and reasons that a diversified yet undivided cosmos points back to an original source in which later differentiations are not yet separated. Admitting many disconnected primal materials would therefore destroy the very undividedness from which the inference proceeds.
Justification, stated as a bridge: the premise of proof five is the world's undivided interconnectedness, so plurality at the root would falsify the premise and not merely complicate the conclusion.
The verdict holds within Sāṃkhya's own inferential licence; a Nyāya atomist declines it by tracing interconnectedness to coordination among many causes rather than to a single origin.
> **Printed question.** “A mango tree is grown out of a mango seed.” How will Sāṃkhya system explain > this process through their theory of causation by rejecting their rival perspectives?
**Demand decoded.** Two obligations. Explain the example through the doctrine of the pre-existent effect *and* reject the rivals by name. An answer without the rival-rejection half cannot score.
**Model answer (357 words).**

Sāṃkhya explains the example by the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in its material cause (**satkāryavāda**), in its specific form as real transformation (**pariṇāmavāda**). The mango tree pre-exists in the mango seed not as a miniature gross tree spatially concealed within it, but as a latent determinate capacity in a material continuum; production is manifestation (**abhivyakti**) of what is latent, and the effect differs from the cause by state (**avasthā**), not by substance.

Five arguments support this. Because a non-entity cannot be produced (**asadakaraṇāt**), no operation yields oil from sand. Because a determinate material cause is taken up (**upādāna-grahaṇāt**), the cultivator selects a mango seed and not sand. Because everything cannot arise from everything (**sarvasambhavābhāvāt**), and non-existence is featureless and therefore indiscriminable, sheer prior absence cannot explain why this seed yields this tree. Because the potent produces only the producible (**śaktasya śakya-karaṇāt**), a potency directed at a determinate effect presupposes that effect as its object. Because the effect has the being of the cause (**kāraṇa-bhāvāt**), the tree continues the seed's material substance as cloth continues threads.

The rivals must now be rejected. Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika holds that the effect is absent beforehand as prior non-existence (**prāgabhāva**) and that production is a new beginning; it objects that Sāṃkhya equivocates between the absolutely non-existent and the merely not-yet-existent, and that the whole (**avayavin**) is a new substance with new properties. Sāṃkhya replies that a not-yet-existent effect must still be something determinate in the cause, else the operation has no terminus, and that new properties are new arrangements (**saṃsthāna**), not new substances from non-being. Advaita agrees that being does not arise from non-being but makes the transformation apparent (**vivartavāda**); Sāṃkhya replies that an appearance-theory cannot explain why production is selective. Buddhism explains becoming by dependent origination without an enduring material root; Sāṃkhya replies that momentary series cannot ground the observed material continuity of seed and tree.
The objection that production becomes pointless is answered by manifestation: effort removes obstruction and supplies conditions rather than creating being.
The doctrine is therefore strongest as an argument about determinacy, and remains contestable only where an opponent grounds determinacy in relational potency instead of latent effect.
> **Printed question.** Explain the Sāṃkhya view on three guṇas (guṇa-traya) and their > modifications.
**Demand decoded.** Two halves of equal weight. The triad is the first half; the two kinds of modification are the second, and omitting them forfeits roughly half the marks.
**Model answer (250 words).**

The three qualities (**guṇa**) are luminosity (**sattva**), activity (**rajas**) and inertia (**tamas**). They are not three separable substances but three inseparable constitutive tendencies of one primordial nature, present together in every evolute in varying proportion.

Luminosity is light, clear and buoyant; its affective tone is pleasure and its function is revelation, clarity and manifestation. Activity is dynamic, restless and projective; its tone is pain and its function is energy, stimulation and movement. Inertia is heavy, obstructive and resistant; its tone is delusion and its function is concealment, resistance and material density. Because character, affective tone and evolutionary function are mapped together, a single triad explains physical constitution, mental state and moral temperament at once — Sāṃkhya's most economical achievement.

Their modification (**guṇa-pariṇāma**) takes two forms. In equilibrium (**sāmyāvasthā**) the three stand in exact balance and nature is unmanifest (**avyakta**); here each quality transforms within its own nature, which is homogeneous modification (**sarūpa-pariṇāma**). This preserves the claim that nature is never inert, so that dissolution is not annihilation. When equilibrium is disturbed in the presence of the conscious witness, the qualities enter asymmetrical relations and generate differentiated evolutes: this is heterogeneous modification (**virūpa-pariṇāma**), to which actual cosmological evolution belongs.
The disturbance is not a mechanical collision. The witness is inactive, so Sāṃkhya describes only functional activation in proximity.

The doctrine is therefore powerful as an account of qualitative variety and weakest exactly at its trigger: what converts homogeneous into heterogeneous modification is presence rather than causation, and Śaṃkara presses precisely this point.
> **Printed question.** Examine and evaluate the proofs given by Sāṃkhya philosophy to prove the > existence of Puruṣa.
**Demand decoded.** Two directives. "Examine" wants the internal logic of the proofs; "evaluate" wants a reasoned judgement on their force. Listing alone answers neither.
**Model answer (194 words).**
Sāṃkhya offers five arguments, all sharing one premise: the entire objective complex is unconscious, instrumental and presented to experience.

Aggregates exist for another (**saṅghāta-parārthatvāt**): body, senses, mind and intellect are complexes, and a complex functions instrumentally for a user distinct from it. The witness must be other than the qualities (**triguṇādi-viparyayāt**): the knower of pleasure, pain and delusion cannot be the same changing states that are known. Organised experience requires a presiding locus (**adhiṣṭhānāt**) — an inference to a conscious witness of lived order, and expressly not a proof of God. Experience requires an enjoyer (**bhoktṛ-bhāvāt**), since presented states demand a subject for whom they appear. Striving for release presupposes a liberable witness (**kaivalyārthaṃ pravṛtteḥ**).

Evaluating them, their force is cumulative rather than individual. Each alone invites a deflationary reply — a Buddhist explains coordination by causal series and ownership by convention — but together they converge on the structural point that a domain of presentation without a subject-pole is not a domain of presentation at all. Their form throughout is general-correlation inference.
Their honest limit is that they establish a subject-pole, not yet an eternal, plural and wholly inactive one.

> **Printed question.** “If Puruṣa and Prakṛti are two completely independent realities, then no > relation between the two is possible.” In the light of this statement make a brief presentation of > Śaṅkara’s criticism of Sāṃkhya dualism.
**Demand decoded.** "Brief presentation … in the light of this statement" means the quoted relation problem must organise the answer, and the criticism must be Śaṃkara's, not a general objection.
**Model answer (190 words).**

The quoted statement isolates Sāṃkhya's contact problem: if the conscious witness is wholly inactive and primordial nature wholly unconscious, no intelligible real relation appears possible, yet evolution, bondage and liberation all presuppose one.

Sāṃkhya answers that the relation is mere proximity (**sānnidhya**), not gross contact: nature becomes active in the witness's mere presence. Two analogies support this — a magnet moves iron without deliberative willing, and a clear crystal appears coloured by a nearby flower without itself changing. The first explains activation by presence; the second explains apparent contamination without real change.

Śaṃkara attacks both. Even a magnet exerts force, so if the witness were genuinely like a magnet it would not be wholly inactive. The crystal may explain appearance, but it cannot explain the initiation of the world-process, since a crystal initiates nothing. He adds that an unconscious chief principle cannot be the Upaniṣadic cause, which is described as conscious and knowing, and that purposive evolution "for the sake of" the witness presupposes intelligence.
His conclusion is that the dualism is unstable: it must either collapse toward monism or admit a third mediating principle — a demand for further explanation rather than a refutation by assertion.
> **Printed question.** Present an account of evolution of Prakṛti as propounded in Sāṃkhyakārikā. > In this context, also explain the difference between buddhi, mahat and ahaṃkāra.

**Demand decoded.** An explicitly split question. The first ten marks are the complete evolutionary sequence; the second ten are the three-term distinction, whose correct answer is that two of the three terms name one principle.
**Model answer (382 words).**

**Part one: the evolution of primordial nature.** Primordial nature (**prakṛti**) is the unmanifest chief principle (**avyakta pradhāna**), one, unconscious and uncreated, constituted by the three qualities in equilibrium. In the mere presence of the conscious witness the equilibrium is disturbed, and heterogeneous modification of the qualities (**virūpa-pariṇāma**) begins.

The first evolute is the great one, also called the determinative intellect (**mahat / buddhi**). From it arises the I-maker (**ahaṃkāra**), the principle of individuation. The I-maker then evolves along two lines. From its luminous aspect arise the coordinating mind (**manas**), the five cognitive capacities — hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell — and the five action capacities: speech, grasping, locomotion, excretion and reproduction. From its inert aspect arise the five subtle elements (**tanmātra**), the potentials of sound, touch, form, taste and smell; and from these arise the five gross elements (**mahābhūta**) — ether, air, fire, water and earth — on the standard correspondence of sound to ether, touch to air, form to fire, taste to water and smell to earth. The active quality supplies energy to both lines and produces no separate set of principles.

Twenty-four evolutes plus the conscious witness give twenty-five principles. The fourfold classification controls the list: nature alone is cause but not effect; the intellect, the I-maker and the five subtle elements are both cause and effect; the mind, the ten capacities and the five gross elements are effects only; and the witness is neither.

**Part two: buddhi, mahat and ahaṃkāra.** The decisive point is that the great one and the determinative intellect are **the same principle** under two names: the great one is its cosmic aspect, the determinative intellect its individual or psychological aspect. Writing them as two successive stages is an error that also corrupts the total count.

The I-maker is genuinely distinct and is derived *from* that first evolute. Functionally, the determinative intellect makes the final ascertainment (**adhyavasāya**) — judgement and discrimination — and, being predominantly luminous and transparent, receives the reflection of the witness. The I-maker appropriates functions as "I" and "mine", and false selfhood crystallises there, which is why it is central to bondage. The coordinating mind, arising later, only synthesises sense-data.
The sequence therefore unifies cosmology and psychology: the equipment of knowing is itself a product of the known.
> **Printed question.** Why does Śaṅkara consider Sāṃkhya Philosophy as his chief opponent (pradhāna > malla)? Examine his arguments against Sāṃkhya Philosophy.

**Demand decoded.** Two halves again. "Why … chief opponent" asks for the grounds of the designation; "examine his arguments" asks for the objections tested for force. Answers that supply only the objections lose the first half entirely.
**Model answer (374 words).**
**Why chief.** The title of chief wrestler (**pradhāna malla**) records systematic strength, not contempt. Three grounds support it.

First, Sāṃkhya is the most sophisticated non-Vedāntic rival at the level of ultimate explanation: it accounts for world, self, bondage, liberation and causation within one coherent metaphysical system, and is therefore near enough to require detailed refutation rather than dismissal. Second, its doctrine of real transformation (**pariṇāmavāda**) is the nearest rival to Advaita's apparent transformation (**vivartavāda**); both deny production from non-being and both derive the world from an ultimate, differing only on whether the derivation is real. Third, both appeal to a single ultimate explanatory ground — Sāṃkhya to one unconscious primal material principle, Advaita to conscious Brahman — so the contest is direct rather than oblique.

**The arguments, examined.** Śaṃkara's first objection is that an unconscious chief principle cannot be the Upaniṣadic cause, since the scriptural source is described as conscious and knowing; "knowing-cause" descriptions exclude an insentient nature. This is powerful within a scripturally governed enquiry, though a non-Vedic opponent may refuse the premise.

His second objection is the contact problem: an inactive witness and an unconscious nature cannot intelligibly relate, yet the whole system depends on their relation. Sāṃkhya answers with mere proximity, supported by the magnet moving iron and the crystal coloured by a nearby flower. Śaṃkara replies that a magnet exerts force — so the analogy either fails or destroys the witness's inactivity — and that the crystal explains appearance but not the initiation of the world-process. This objection is the strongest, because the two analogies do different jobs and neither does both.

His third objection is teleological: if nature evolves "for the sake of" the witness, purposiveness appears to require intelligence. Sāṃkhya replies that purposive functioning need not be conscious planning, as milk flows for the calf; the reply preserves internal sufficiency but does not remove the pressure.

**Verdict.** Śaṃkara treats Sāṃkhya as chief opponent because it attempts, from an unconscious first principle, exactly what Advaita attempts from a conscious one. He rejects it because the ultimate cause must be conscious, teleology cannot rest on unconscious nature, and the witness–nature relation remains unstable — a demonstration that the dualism needs further explanation rather than a proof that Advaita is thereby established.
> **Printed question.** Does the seed contain the tree? Discuss with reference to Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika > Philosophy.
**Routing note.** Primary ownership lies with Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, but the question is unanswerable without the Sāṃkhya position it is framed against, and the Sāṃkhya side must be stated accurately.
**Model answer (188 words).**

For Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika the answer is no. Before production the effect is characterised by prior non-existence (**prāgabhāva**) in its material cause; production is a genuinely new beginning (**ārambhavāda**), and the resulting whole (**avayavin**) is a new substance inhering in its parts and possessing properties the parts lack — a cloth covers, whereas separate threads do not.

The question is framed against Sāṃkhya, which answers yes on its own terms: the effect pre-exists as a latent determinate capacity, since non-existence is featureless and cannot explain why this seed yields this tree, and since a potency directed at a determinate effect presupposes that effect. Sāṃkhya does not claim that a miniature gross tree is spatially hidden in the seed.

Nyāya's reply is that Sāṃkhya equivocates: it denies only that the tree exists *as* the tree beforehand, not that the seed is determinate. Determinacy is secured instead by the causal capacity of the material and by the exclusion of non-causal antecedents.
The dispute therefore turns on whether determinacy can be carried by a relational potency alone, or must be grounded in a latent effect — a difference of first principles rather than of evidence.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### 2021 · Q5(a) · 10 marks · routed

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: > **Printed question.** Do you agree with the view that ‘Vivartavāda is the logical development of > Pariṇāmavāda’? Give reasons in support of your answer.
**Routing note.** Owned by Vedānta, but the question is a direct examination of whether Sāṃkhya's real transformation entails Advaita's apparent transformation.
**Model answer (181 words).**
I agree only partly, and the qualification carries the argument.

The claim is defensible in one respect. Both doctrines deny production from sheer non-being, so both belong to a broad pre-existence orientation; and apparent transformation can be presented as the result of pressing real transformation's own logic — if the ultimate must not be diminished by producing, transformation is best read as appearance rather than as real change.

It is indefensible in another. Real transformation is not an incomplete version of apparent transformation but a rival with opposite commitments. Sāṃkhya's cause is unconscious primordial nature and its world is a real evolute; Advaita's cause is conscious Brahman and its world is ultimately appearance. Sāṃkhya's mechanism is the modification of the three qualities; Advaita's is superimposition. Treating one as the logical development of the other therefore assumes the very Vedāntic premise — that an ultimate cannot really change — which Sāṃkhya explicitly denies by defining nature as that whose being is modification.
The view is thus historically suggestive as a description of Vedāntic self-understanding, but logically question-begging as a claim about entailment.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### 2022 · Q5(e) · 10 marks · routed

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: > **Printed question.** Write a note on Nyāya notion of Prāgabhāva (prior non-existence). How does > this notion help Naiyāyikas in defending their position on causation against the Sāṃkhya view of > causation? Critically discuss.
**Routing note.** Owned by Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika; the second and third clauses make Sāṃkhya's causal doctrine the subject under test, so the Sāṃkhya side must be argued and not merely named.
**Model answer (296 words).**

Prior non-existence (**prāgabhāva**) is one of the four absences recognised in the Vaiśeṣika category-scheme. It is the absence of an effect in its material cause before production: beginningless but with an end, since it terminates precisely when the effect is produced. Every absence has a counter-positive, and here the counter-positive is the effect itself.

The notion does exact defensive work for Nyāya's doctrine that the effect does not pre-exist (**asatkāryavāda**). It gives a positive account of the pre-production situation, so production becomes the destruction of prior non-existence rather than creation from nothing; it preserves the reality of production, since something genuinely new begins; and it blocks the charge of arbitrariness, because determinacy is located in the causal capacity of the material and in the exclusion of non-causal antecedents rather than in a latent effect.

Against Sāṃkhya it grounds a dilemma. If the effect exists beforehand, the causal operation is idle; if it does not exist as the effect, Nyāya's position has been conceded, and prior non-existence names exactly what the effect then lacks. Nyāya adds that the whole is a new substance with properties its parts lack.

Sāṃkhya replies that a merely negative antecedent cannot discriminate outcomes, since non-existence is featureless; that production is manifestation (**abhivyakti**) and effort removes obstruction; and that cause and effect differ by state (**avasthā**) rather than by substance, so the operation is not idle.

Critically, prior non-existence answers the charge of creation from nothing but relocates rather than removes the demand for determinacy, which Nyāya must then discharge through causal capacity — the very notion Sāṃkhya claims is unintelligible without a latent effect.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### ORIGINAL SOLVED MAINS PRACTICE

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: > **Question.** Explain why Sāṃkhya restricts the means of valid knowledge to three, and show how > this restriction shapes its metaphysics.
**Model answer (177 words).**

Sāṃkhya admits exactly three instruments of knowledge — perception, inference and reliable testimony — and reduces comparison, postulation, non-apprehension, inclusion and traditional report to these three rather than rejecting them as worthless. Comparison operates through a prior verbal report applied inferentially; postulation is inference to the best explanatory condition; non-apprehension belongs to the failure-conditions of perception.

This restriction is not economy for its own sake; it creates an obligation. Both ultimates — primordial nature and the conscious witness — are beyond the senses (**atīndriya**), so perception cannot reach them, and testimony alone would beg the question against a non-Vedic opponent. Imperceptibility itself is disarmed by the standard list of causes of non-perception, in which root nature falls under subtlety (**saukṣmya**).

The whole evidential weight therefore falls on general-correlation inference (**sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa**), which alone can reach a term whose invariable relation was never observed directly. The five proofs of nature and the five proofs of the witness are precisely the shape this epistemology forces.
The metaphysics is thus epistemically driven — and correspondingly vulnerable if that inferential licence is denied, as Cārvāka denies it.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### Original 1 · 10 marks

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: > **Question.** "Nothing happens to Puruṣa at liberation." Comment on this statement with reference > to the Sāṃkhya account of bondage and kaivalya.
**Model answer (180 words).**
The statement is accurate in strict Sāṃkhya and is the best available formulation of its soteriology.

Bondage is non-discrimination (**aviveka**) between the witness and nature. The determinative intellect, being transparent, receives the reflection of consciousness, and false appropriation (**abhimāna**) follows — "I am the doer, knower, enjoyer". Since this is misattribution and not modification, the witness is not really altered by bondage.

Liberation is correspondingly cognitive. Discriminative knowledge (**viveka-jñāna**) stabilises the distinction between witness-consciousness and quality-evolutes, false identification ends, and the resulting state is isolation (**kaivalya**) — disentanglement, not merger and not annihilation. The canonical image is the dancer who retires once she has been seen; the potter's wheel explains why the body continues by prior momentum, giving liberation while living (**jīvanmukti**) before final release (**videhamukti**).
The strict formulation follows: the witness is never really bound, liberated or transmigrating, since these belong to nature and the subtle body.
The comment must end with the cost. If nothing happens to the witness, the school must explain in what sense the problem was ever *its* problem — a clarification it offers but does not demonstrate.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### Original 2 · 10 marks

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: > **Question.** Examine the claim that Sāṃkhya's theory of the three qualities makes cosmology and > psychology a single subject.
**Model answer (270 words).**
The claim is substantially correct and identifies Sāṃkhya's most economical achievement, though it must be stated with care.

The three qualities are luminosity, activity and inertia: not three substances but three inseparable constitutive tendencies of one nature, present together in every evolute in varying proportion. Each is defined simultaneously along three registers — character, affective tone and evolutionary function. Luminosity is buoyant, carries pleasure and performs manifestation; activity is restless, carries pain and performs movement; inertia is heavy, carries delusion and performs concealment.

Because a single triad is defined across physical, affective and functional registers at once, the same explanatory apparatus accounts for the density of a stone, the dullness of a mind and the confusion of a temperament. The evolutionary sequence completes the unification: intellect, I-maker, mind and the ten capacities are evolutes of the same nature that yields the subtle and gross elements, so the equipment of knowing is itself a product of the known.

Two qualifications are needed. First, the unification is achieved by placing all mental functioning inside unconscious nature, which is why Sāṃkhya is a consciousness–nature dualism and not a mind–body dualism; the psychology it unifies with cosmology is a psychology *without* consciousness. Second, the unification does not extend to the witness, which is beyond the qualities altogether, so exactly one thing remains outside the single subject.

Examined, then, the claim holds for everything the qualities constitute and fails precisely at the point where Sāṃkhya's dualism begins. That is not a defect in the theory of the qualities but the boundary the theory was designed to respect — and it is also where the system's relation problem starts.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### Original 3 · 15 marks

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: > **Question.** Critically examine whether the Sāṃkhya doctrine of many Puruṣas is proved or merely > postulated.
**Model answer (277 words).**
Sāṃkhya argues for the plurality of witnesses rather than assuming it, but the arguments establish less than the doctrine requires, so the honest verdict is "argued, not demonstrated".

The case rests on three arguments of *Sāṃkhyakārikā* 18. The fixed distribution of birth, death and sense-faculties: one witness would mean one birth is every birth. The non-simultaneity of activity: beings act at different times, whereas one self would make all streams act together. Differential constitution by the qualities: temperaments differ as luminous, active or inert. A fourth consideration, differential liberation, is a supplementary inference and not a phrase of that verse.

These arguments share a form: they infer transcendental plurality from empirical non-transferability. That form is exactly what Advaita contests. Śaṃkara replies that every cited difference belongs to limiting adjuncts (**upādhi**) — bodies, minds and quality-configurations — and that pure consciousness, being without attribute, part, action or location, admits no principle of individuation; Sāṃkhya therefore proves at most a plurality of mental streams (**citta**).

Sāṃkhya's counter is that bondage and release are non-transferable and that the reflection model requires distinct loci in distinct intellects. This is a genuine reply, since Advaita must then treat bondage itself as adventitious and the many empirical selves as apparent.

The residual difficulty is internal and should be conceded. If every witness is qualitatively identical, the school cannot say what makes them numerically many; plurality is inferred from non-transferable experience rather than grounded in a stated principle of individuation.

Critically examined, the doctrine is therefore well motivated and under-demonstrated: it is proved as far as moral and experiential individuality can prove anything, and postulated precisely where metaphysical individuation is demanded.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### Original 4 · 15 marks

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: > **Question.** Analyse the relation between Sāṃkhya's epistemology, its theory of causation and its > account of liberation, and assess whether the three form a coherent system.
**Model answer (368 words).**

**The three parts.** Sāṃkhya's epistemology admits three instruments — perception, inference and reliable testimony — and reduces all other candidates to them. Its causal doctrine holds that the effect pre-exists in its material cause (**satkāryavāda**) in the specific form of real transformation (**pariṇāmavāda**), effected by the modification of the three qualities. Its soteriology holds that bondage is non-discrimination and liberation is discriminative knowledge issuing in isolation (**kaivalya**).

**How epistemology drives causation.** Because both ultimates are beyond the senses, the entire evidential burden falls on general-correlation inference. That is why the five proofs of primordial nature exist at all — and the third of them, from operation due to causal power (**śaktitaḥ pravṛtteś ca**), is already a causal thesis. Determinate production is the datum from which the material root is inferred, and determinate production is what the doctrine of the pre-existent effect explains. Epistemology and causation are therefore two descriptions of one inference.

**How causation drives soteriology.** Real transformation makes the world a genuine evolute rather than an appearance, so bondage and release are events in a real order. But real transformation also places intellect, I-maker and mind inside nature, which produces the reflection model: transparent intellect receives the witness's reflection and false appropriation follows. Liberation must then be the correction of an attribution rather than the destruction of an entity — which is exactly why isolation is disentanglement rather than merger, and why the dancer image, not the prison image, is canonical.

**How soteriology returns to epistemology.** The fifth proof of the witness — that striving for release presupposes a liberable witness — makes the soteriology part of the evidence. The system closes on itself.

**Assessment.** The coherence is genuine and unusually tight: each part supplies a premise the next requires, and the enumeration of twenty-five principles is simultaneously a cosmology, a psychology and the content of liberating knowledge.

The incoherence, where it appears, is concentrated at one joint. The disturbance of equilibrium is attributed to mere presence, which is neither perception, nor inference from causal power, nor a real transformation — the three things the system otherwise relies on.
Sāṃkhya is therefore coherent as a system of explanation and under-determined at its point of origination, which is precisely where Śaṃkara concentrates his attack.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### Original 5 · 20 marks

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: > **Question.** "Sāṃkhya purchases the inactivity of consciousness at a high price." Discuss with > reference to agency, moral responsibility and rebirth.
**Model answer (372 words).**
The statement is correct, and the price is best displayed by following one commitment through three consequences.

**The commitment.** The conscious witness is pure, self-luminous, inactive and changeless consciousness, wholly beyond the three qualities. Every productive function belongs to nature. This is not an incidental thesis: it is what the proofs of the witness establish and what makes liberation possible, since a really modified witness could never be restored.

**First consequence: agency.** Agency must be relocated entirely to nature's evolutes. The determinative intellect ascertains, the I-maker appropriates, the mind coordinates — and all three are insentient. What we experience as conscious agency is the two-way appearance: the insentient organ appears conscious, and the inactive witness appears to be an agent. Nyāya objects that an agentless self is otiose and makes its own self a substance with adventitious cognition, volition and effort. Sāṃkhya's reply is uncompromising: ascribing agency to the witness is precisely the false appropriation (**abhimāna**) in which bondage consists.

**Second consequence: moral responsibility.** If the witness never acts, it cannot straightforwardly own a moral career. Sāṃkhya secures desert through the stable association of one subtle stream with one numerically distinct witness. But this is asserted rather than derived, and it inherits the school's deepest difficulty: qualitatively identical witnesses have no stated principle of individuation, so the very individuality that moral ownership requires is the thing least well grounded.

**Third consequence: rebirth.** Transmigration must be relocated too. The subtle body — eighteen constituents: determinative intellect, I-maker, the eleven capacities including the mind, and the five subtle elements — carries dispositions and karmic tendencies, conditioned by the intellect's eight tendencies of merit and demerit, knowledge and ignorance, detachment and non-detachment, power and powerlessness. The gross body from parental material falls away. The witness neither acts nor literally migrates.

**Assessment.** The price is real but the purchase is deliberate. Inactivity buys a clean separation of phenomenal consciousness from cognitive processing, an intelligible account of liberation as correction rather than escape, and a non-theistic explanation of bondage. It costs an unowned agency, an ungrounded principle of individuation and a rebirth without a traveller.
Whether the price is too high depends on the prior question the schools actually divide on: whether consciousness may be described as doing anything at all.

## 0A. SĀṂKHYA EPISTEMOLOGY — PRAMĀṆA AND COGNITION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ Sāṃkhya admits exactly **three pramāṇas** (valid means of knowledge): **dṛṣṭa / pratyakṣa** (perception), **anumāna** (inference) and **āptavacana / śabda** (reliable testimony).

**Statement.** ✅ Other proposed pramāṇas — **upamāna** (comparison), **arthāpatti** (postulation), **anupalabdhi** (non-apprehension), **sambhava** (inclusion/probability) and **aitihya** (traditional report) — are not rejected as useless; they are reduced to, or included within, these three.

**Exam use.** ⚠️ This epistemology is the hinge of the whole system: because **mūla-prakṛti** (root Prakṛti) and **puruṣa** are not sense-objects, Sāṃkhya must show how they can still be known without multiplying pramāṇas.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### 0A.1 The three-pramāṇa scheme

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ **Dṛṣṭa / pratyakṣa** is the **prativiṣayādhyavasāya** (ascertainment with respect to a presented object) of objects through the sense-capacities in contact with them.
**Distinction.** ✅ **Anumāna** is threefold:
**pūrvavat** | ✅ From an antecedent cause/sign to a later effect | ✅ Clouds → likely rain
**śeṣavat** | ✅ From an effect/residue back to its cause or wider ground | ✅ Tasting one drop of seawater → seawater is salty
**sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa** | ✅ From a general correlation where the connection between the terms is not itself directly perceived | ✅ Seeing the sun in different positions → the sun moves
**Statement.** ✅ **Āptavacana / śabda** is the word of a trustworthy source, pre-eminently **Veda / śruti**, where the speaker or text is not defective and the object is not otherwise easily known.

| Type of anumāna | Meaning | Example |

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **upamāna** | ✅ Included in inference/testimony | ✅ Similarity works because a prior verbal report is applied inferentially to a present case.
**arthāpatti** | ✅ Included in inference | ✅ Postulation is an inference to the best explanatory condition; it does not need a separate instrument.

**anupalabdhi** | ✅ Included under perception's failure-conditions, not a separate pramāṇa | ✅ Non-perception means the conditions for perceiving the object are absent or the object is unavailable; no new instrument is required.
**sambhava** | ✅ Included in inference | ✅ Inclusion from a larger unit to a smaller or probable implication is inferential dependence.
**aitihya** | ✅ Included in testimony when reliable, otherwise rejected | ✅ Mere tradition has force only when it becomes trustworthy verbal cognition.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ **Avyakta / mūla-prakṛti** and **puruṣa** are both **atīndriya** (beyond the senses): neither is an object of ordinary perception.

**Statement.** ✅ Their imperceptibility is not proof of non-existence; the standard non-perception discussion assigns mūla-prakṛti's imperceptibility to **saukṣmya** (subtlety), and Puruṣa is likewise atīndriya rather than non-existent.

**Distinction.** ✅ Sāṃkhya lists standard causes of non-perception: excessive distance, excessive proximity, defect of the organ, inattention of mind, subtlety, obstruction by an intervening object, being overpowered by something else, and admixture with like things.

**Argument.** ⚠️ Since perception cannot reach atīndriya entities, and testimony alone would beg the question against non-Vedic opponents, the argumentative burden falls on **anumāna**, specifically **sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa anumāna**.

**Argument.** ⚠️ Sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa inference can reach a term that is in principle imperceptible because it does not require the vyāpti (invariable relation) to be established by seeing both terms together; it works through a general correlation of kinds.

**Conclusion.** ⚠️ Therefore the five arguments for Prakṛti and the arguments for Puruṣa are not rhetorical flourishes; they discharge an epistemological obligation created by Sāṃkhya's own three-pramāṇa scheme.

**Exam use.** ⚠️ A strong answer should write: **Sāṃkhya first restricts pramāṇas to three, then uses sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa inference to justify the two entities that perception cannot give — Prakṛti and Puruṣa.**

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### 0A.4 Why sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa inference is decisive

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Presupposition.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya presupposes that inference from general correlation can legitimately reach an entity of a kind never itself observed as a sense-object.
**Objection.** ❓ **Cārvāka:** vyāpti cannot be secured for a term never perceived; therefore inference to mūla-prakṛti or puruṣa is speculative.

**Reply.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya answers that strict perceptualism cannot explain ordinary causal reasoning either; manifest, dependent, purposive and objectifiable experience demands an unmanifest material ground and a conscious witness.

**Objection.** ❓ **Nyāya:** sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa inference is legitimate, but Sāṃkhya overuses it; a plurality of atoms plus an intelligent Īśvara explains the ordered world more economically than an unobservable material first cause.

**Reply.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya replies that the continuity between cause and effect, the guṇa-character of experience, and the determinacy of production are better explained by a single material Prakṛti; adding Īśvara is unnecessary because it does not explain the material continuity itself.

decisions.heading: 0A.6 Theory of cognition: antaḥkaraṇa and reflection

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ The **antaḥkaraṇa** (inner instrument) has three functions: **buddhi** (determinative intellect), **ahaṃkāra** (I-maker) and **manas** (coordinating mind).

**Statement.** ✅ The full **trayodaśa-karaṇa** (thirteen-fold instrument) consists of 3 internal organs + 5 **buddhīndriyas / jñānendriyas** (cognitive sense-capacities) + 5 **karmendriyas** (action-capacities).
**buddhi** | ✅ Final ascertainment (**adhyavasāya**), judgement, discrimination
**ahaṃkāra** | ✅ Appropriation as "I" and "mine"
**manas** | ✅ Coordination, attention, synthesis of sense-data
**five buddhīndriyas** | ✅ Cognitive access to sound, touch, form, taste and smell
**five karmendriyas** | ✅ Speech, grasping, movement, excretion and reproduction/action-functions

**Distinction.** ✅ The external faculties function as **dvāra** (doors), while the inner organ functions as **dvārin** (doorkeeper/door-supervisor) because it receives, coordinates and determines what enters cognition.
**Statement.** ✅ **Buddhi alone makes the final ascertainment (adhyavasāya)**; manas only coordinates and ahaṃkāra only appropriates.

**Argument.** ✅ Buddhi is sattva-predominant and therefore transparent; it reflects Puruṣa's consciousness through **puruṣa-cchāyā-āpatti / buddhi-pratibimba** (falling of Puruṣa's shadow/reflection in buddhi).
**Conclusion.** ⚠️ Cognition seems conscious although buddhi is **jaḍa** (insentient), because reflected consciousness illuminates buddhi's operations.
**Statement.** ✅ This reflection generates **abhimāna** (false appropriation: "I am the doer/knower/enjoyer"), and that abhimāna is the psychological root of bondage.

**Two-way appearance.** ✅ Through the conjunction or semblance of conjunction, the unconscious internal instrument appears conscious, while the inactive Puruṣa appears to be an agent. Productive agency belongs to the qualities and evolutes of Prakṛti; witnessing belongs to Puruṣa.
**Exam use.** ⚠️ For Sāṃkhya, the mind does not know by itself and Puruṣa does not act by itself; empirical knowing is a reflected-consciousness event in buddhi.

| Presupposition | Why it matters |

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Objection.** ❓ **Advaita / Śaṃkara:** every difference cited is a difference in **upādhis** (limiting adjuncts — bodies, minds, guṇa-configurations), not in consciousness itself. Pure consciousness, being without attribute, part, action or spatial location, admits no principle of individuation; therefore Sāṃkhya proves at most a plurality of **cittas** (mental streams), not Puruṣas.

**Reply.** ✅ Sāṃkhya replies that if there were one Puruṣa, the bondage of one would be the bondage of all and the release of one the release of all; the reflection model also requires distinct reflected loci in distinct buddhis.

**Residual force.** ⚠️ Advaita answers that bondage itself is adventitious and the many jīvas are apparent, so the exchange terminates in a clash of first principles: Sāṃkhya trusts the plurality given in experience, while Advaita subordinates plurality to the unity given in śruti.

**Objection.** ❓ **Nyāya:** Nyāya agrees that selves are many, but objects to a purely inactive self; an agent-less self cannot be the locus of moral desert, so Nyāya makes ātman a substance with adventitious cognition, volition and effort.
**Reply.** ✅ Sāṃkhya replies that agency belongs to Prakṛti's evolutes; ascribing agency to Puruṣa is precisely the **abhimāna** that bondage consists in.
**Objection.** ❓ **Buddhist:** a permanent, changeless and actionless entity is causally idle and therefore, by **arthakriyā** (efficacy), unreal.

**Reply.** ✅ Sāṃkhya replies that Puruṣa's efficacy is not productive causation but **sannidhi / sānnidhya** (mere presence) that renders Prakṛti's activity experienced; without Puruṣa the teleology of Prakṛti (**puruṣārtha**) is unintelligible.
**Objection.** ❓ **Internal objection:** if Puruṣas are all identical in nature — pure, attributeless consciousness — what makes them numerically many?

**Reply.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya's honest answer is that plurality is inferred from the non-transferability of experience, bondage and liberation, but the ultimate individuation of qualitatively identical Puruṣas remains the school's weakest joint.

## 4. CAUSATION — PRE-EXISTENCE OF THE EFFECT (SATKĀRYAVĀDA)

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: - ✅ **Satkāryavāda** holds that the effect pre-exists in its material cause.
- ✅ Production is manifestation, not creation out of sheer non-being.
- ✅ Sāṃkhya's specific form of satkāryavāda is **pariṇāmavāda**, the doctrine of real transformation.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### 4.1 Statement

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ The standard Sāṃkhya set gives five reasons for holding that the effect pre-exists in its material cause.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### 4.2 The five arguments for satkāryavāda

decisions.heading: (1) **asadakaraṇāt** — because what does not exist cannot be brought into being

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ A sheer non-entity cannot be produced.
**Argument.** ✅ No amount of causal operation can produce a hare's horn or oil from sand; production presupposes something determinate to be produced.
**Example.** ✅ A potter's effort can manifest a pot from clay, but it cannot manifest a square circle from nothing.
**Objection.** ❓ **Nyāya:** Sāṃkhya equivocates between the absolutely non-existent and the merely not-yet-existent; Nyāya denies only that the pot exists as a pot before production.
**Reply.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya presses that the "not-yet-existent" effect must still be something in the material cause, otherwise the operation would have no determinate terminus.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### (1) **asadakaraṇāt** — because what does not exist cannot be brought into being

decisions.heading: (2) **upādāna-grahaṇāt** — because a determinate material cause is taken up

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ Specific effects require specific material causes.
**Argument.** ✅ One who wants curd takes milk, not water; one who wants cloth takes threads, not clay.
**Example.** ✅ The selection of mango seed rather than sand for a mango tree shows a determinate causal base.
**Objection.** ❓ The restriction may be explained by causal capacity rather than by the pre-existence of the effect.
**Reply.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya replies that causal capacity in the required determinate sense just is the latent presence of that effect in that material continuum.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### (2) **upādāna-grahaṇāt** — because a determinate material cause is taken up

decisions.heading: (3) **sarvasambhavābhāvāt** — because everything cannot arise from everything

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ If effects were wholly non-existent before production, any cause could produce any effect.
**Argument.** ✅ Non-existence as such is indistinguishable; therefore it cannot explain why curd arises from milk and not from water.
**Example.** ✅ Cloth comes from threads, not from milk; curd comes from milk, not from threads.
**Objection.** ❓ A rival can say that restrictions come from the constitution of causes, not from effects already existing in causes.
**Reply.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya replies that a constitution capable of producing only X is precisely the latent presence of X as a determinate effect-potential.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### (3) **sarvasambhavābhāvāt** — because everything cannot arise from everything

decisions.heading: (4) **śaktasya śakya-karaṇāt** — because the efficient can produce only what it is capable of producing

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ A cause has a determinate **śakti** (potency) directed toward a determinate effect.
**Argument.** ✅ A potency for X is unintelligible unless X is in some manner already there as the object of that potency.
**Example.** ✅ Milk has the potency for curd, not for cloth; threads have the potency for cloth, not for curd.
**Objection.** ❓ **Nyāya:** potency is a relational property of the cause, not the effect in latent form.
**Reply.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya replies that a merely relational potency cannot explain determinate production unless the producible form is already grounded in the material cause.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### (4) **śaktasya śakya-karaṇāt** — because the efficient can produce only what it is capable of producing

decisions.heading: (5) **kāraṇa-bhāvāt** — because the effect has the nature/being of the cause

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ The effect is non-different from the cause in substance.
**Argument.** ✅ Cloth is nothing over and above threads in a certain arrangement; it has the same material basis, weight and guṇa-continuity.
**Example.** ✅ Ornament and gold differ in form and name, but the material substance remains gold.
**Objection.** ❓ **Nyāya:** the whole (**avayavin**) is a new substance with new properties; a cloth covers, but separate threads do not.
**Reply.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya replies that the new properties are new **saṃsthāna** (arrangements/configurations), not new substances created out of non-being.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: #### (5) **kāraṇa-bhāvāt** — because the effect has the nature/being of the cause

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Statement.** ✅ Sāṃkhya's satkāryavāda is specifically **pariṇāmavāda**: the effect is a real transformation of the cause.
**Distinction.** ✅ It is not **vivartavāda**, because the world is not a mere appearance superimposed on an unchanged cause; it is the real evolution of Prakṛti.
**Argument.** ✅ The mechanism is **guṇa-pariṇāma**: the three guṇas transform and recombine to produce the differentiated tattvas.

**Distinction.** ✅ In **sarūpa-pariṇāma**, each guṇa transforms homogeneously within its own nature during **pralaya** or equilibrium; in **virūpa-pariṇāma**, the guṇas transform heterogeneously and generate the manifest evolutes.
**Objection.** ❓ If the effect already exists, causal effort becomes pointless.
**Reply.** ✅ Production is **abhivyakti** (manifestation) of what is latent; effort removes obstruction and supplies conditions, it does not create being out of non-being.
**Objection.** ❓ Satkāryavāda abolishes the distinction between cause and effect.
**Reply.** ✅ Cause and effect differ by **avasthā** (state): the cause is latent/unmanifest, the effect is patent/manifest.
**Objection.** ❓ Satkāryavāda implies the world was always exactly as it is now.
**Reply.** ✅ Sāṃkhya denies that the gross effect is already manifest; only the determinate capacity/effect-form exists latently in the cause.
**Exam use.** ⚠️ The mango-seed example should be written as latent effect + material continuity + real transformation, not as a miniature gross mango tree hidden inside the seed.

## 5. LIBERATION (KAIVALYA)

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: Sāṃkhya inquiry begins from the impact of threefold suffering (**duḥkha-traya**):
1. internal or psychophysical suffering (**ādhyātmika**) — bodily disease and mental affliction;
2. suffering caused by other beings or external natural agents (**ādhibhautika**) — injury from humans, animals and material surroundings;
3. suffering attributed to cosmic, elemental or unseen agencies (**ādhidaivika**) — environmental or supernormal affliction in the traditional classification.
- ✅ Ordinary remedies and ritual means offer incomplete or temporary relief; discriminative knowledge aims at final and non-returning cessation.
- ⚠️ The threefold diagnosis is not a separate printed noun, but it explains why liberation is the practical end of the entire system.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: - ✅ No God is required for either bondage or liberation in classical Sāṃkhya.

- ✅ Standard anti-theistic arguments add:
1. if God acts from desire or selfish motive, God is not perfect or free;
2. if God is eternally fulfilled, there is no motive to create a painful world;
3. if God distributes results under karma, divine independence is limited; if distribution is arbitrary, justice fails;
4. an immutable conscious God cannot be the material source of a changing unconscious world under Sāṃkhya's cause-effect continuity;
5. eternal Puruṣas and primordial nature already explain consciousness and material evolution without a creator hypothesis.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: - ✅ If Puruṣa is inactive and Prakṛti is unconscious, how can they relate at all?

- ✅ Puruṣa does not push or alter Prakṛti by action.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### 6.2 Sāṃkhya response: proximity, not physical contact

- ✅ **Crystal and flower:** as a clear crystal appears coloured by a nearby flower without itself changing, Puruṣa appears affected by Prakṛti without real transformation.
- ⚠️ The first analogy explains activation by presence; the second explains apparent contamination without real change.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### 6.3 Analogies

- ✅ The magnet analogy fails because even a magnet exerts force; if Puruṣa were like that, it would not be wholly inactive.
- ✅ The crystal analogy may explain appearance, but not the initiation of world-process.
- ✅ Therefore Sāṃkhya dualism appears unstable: either it collapses toward monism or it requires a third mediating principle.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: - ✅ Mahat and buddhi are the SAME tattva — mahat is the cosmic name, buddhi is the individual/psychological name. They are NOT two separate stages.

## 11F. GRADED VERDICT ON SĀṂKHYA

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: - ✅ Sāṃkhya is a rigorously argued non-theistic realism rather than a loose mythology of evolution.
- ✅ Its guṇa theory is one of the most economical Indian accounts of qualitative variety.
- ✅ Satkāryavāda is a genuinely powerful causal thesis because it explains determinate production and material continuity.
- ✅ Its separation of consciousness from mental function anticipates the modern distinction between phenomenal consciousness and cognitive processing.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### 11F.1 What is strong

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: - ⚠️ The puruṣa–prakṛti relation is under-explained because inactive consciousness and unconscious matter must somehow generate experience.
- ⚠️ Unconscious teleology remains difficult: Prakṛti works "for" Puruṣa without intelligence.
- ⚠️ Individuation of attributeless Puruṣas is the weakest point in the plurality doctrine.
- ⚠️ The beginning of bondage is obscure because Puruṣa is never really modified and Prakṛti is beginningless.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### 11F.2 What is weak

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: - ❓ Whether early Sāṃkhya was originally theistic or consistently nirīśvara remains debated.
- ❓ Whether kaivalya is purely negative isolation or has a positive phenomenological character is disputed.
- ❓ The relation between the Kārikā tradition and later Sūtra tradition is historically and doctrinally contested.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### 11F.3 What is genuinely contested

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: - **10 marks.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya is strongest as a concise dualist realism: one Prakṛti explains the world, many Puruṣas explain experience, and viveka explains liberation.
- **15 marks.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya's power lies in the mutual fit of pramāṇa, satkāryavāda, guṇa theory and kaivalya, though its contact problem invites Vedāntic criticism.

- **20 marks.** ⚠️ Sāṃkhya is a philosophically serious non-theistic system whose causal realism and psychology of reflection are impressive, but whose unconscious teleology and plurality of attributeless Puruṣas remain unresolved pressure points.
